speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This Bill focuses on the first category of salary-related disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Today, there are three avenues for resolving them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Union members in unionised companies have recourse to conciliation under the Industrial Relations Act (IRA) and access to the Industrial Arbitration Court (IAC).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Even though most of them are currently rank-and-file workers, but with the IRA amendments passed in 2015, we now allow more professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) to have access to this route.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Second, employees who are covered by the Employment Act (EA) ‒ these are rank-and-file employees and PMEs earning up to $4,500 per month ‒ regardless of whether they are union members, they have access to what is commonly called "the Labour Court" at the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Third, all employees have access to the civil Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This recourse is important, especially for complex claims which may require legal representation and take longer to resolve.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This is especially so amongst PMEs, whose number has increased by about 20% over the last decade and is set to grow further.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: ECT will take over the Labour Court's function of hearing statutory salary-related disputes on employee entitlements under the Retirement & Re-employment Act (RRA) and the Child Development Co-Savings Act (CDCA).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: These include unpaid salary, overtime pay, salary in lieu of notice, employment assistance payment and maternity benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In addition, the ECT will hear contractual salary-related claims from employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Such claims include payment of allowances, bonuses, commissions, salary in lieu of notice and retrenchment benefits, provided that these are expressed in monetary terms in the contract.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The ECT will also hear claims from the employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: However, as with the Labour Court, employers can only bring claims for notice pay to the ECT.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The types of claims which the ECT can hear are laid out in the First and Second Schedules of the Bill, which may be updated based on 	Page: 79 tripartite consultations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Besides hearing more types of claims, the ECT will be accessible to more employees, compared to the existing Labour Court.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: With this, all employees can now have access to the ECT for their statutory and/or contractual salary-related disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Public servants, domestic workers and seafarers will continue to be able to bring their statutory salary-related claims regarding employment assistance payment and maternity benefits to the ECT, just as for the Labour Court.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As per current practice at the Labour Court, contractual salary-related claims of these groups of employees will not be heard at the ECT.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Public servants continue to have recourse through the Public Service's internal processes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Domestic workers can approach their employment agencies and MOM to resolve employment disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Likewise, for seafarers, they can continue to settle disputes, including salary-related disputes, under the Merchant Shipping (Maritime Labour Convention) Act.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I will now describe how the ECT will work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The ECT will be set up under the State Courts, with the claims to be heard by legally-qualified Tribunal Magistrates and in accordance with Court processes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We have built in features to keep the process expeditious and affordable.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: All parties will be required to go through mediation conducted by MOM-approved mediators before their claims can be heard at ECT.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This is because, from our experience, it shows that mediation is an effective way of resolving salary-related claims amicably between the parties.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The claimant must submit a request for mediation within one year after the claim arises, or within six months if the employment relationship has ended.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: There will be no legal representation, as with the Labour Court and Small Claims Tribunals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If mediation is successful, parties will sign a settlement agreement and apply for the registration of the settlement agreement in the District Courts for it to be enforceable as a binding Court Order.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If mediation is unsuccessful, the mediator will issue a referral certificate for the claimant to lodge a claim at ECT.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Even so, the tripartite partners will continue to have important roles to play.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: For a start, TADM will conduct the pre-ECT mediation and serve as the MOM-approved mediation centre for all employees, both unionised and non-unionised members.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Union members today enjoy additional remedies, such as the Tripartite Mediation Framework (TMF), MOM conciliation or recourse to the Industrial Arbitration Court.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are also amending the IRA to expand the coverage of TMF so that more union members can use this avenue to resolve more types of disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Today, only managers and executives earning up to $4,500 per month who are union members in non-unionised companies have access to the TMF.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We will remove the salary cap and also allow the rank-and-file employees to access the TMF.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In addition, in recognition of the role of the unions, we have included three features in the ECT process.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Second, union members in unionised companies can be represented by their unions at mediation and at the ECT, and this will be as prescribed in the subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Third, union members in non-unionised companies who undergo TMF can seek consent from the ECT to have their tripartite mediation advisors observe their ECT hearings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I also thank our tripartite partner, the Singapore National Employers' Federation (SNEF), for strongly supporting the setting up of ECT.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the growing number of PMEs in Singapore, I recall mooting the idea of setting up an ECT with our Tripartite Partners four years ago to look into mediating and resolving employment disputes, and I am elated that it is going to come into fruition.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The setting up of the ECT is a landmark development in the area of employment law and industrial relations practice in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The new ECT will be able to hear claims from all employees, regardless of their salary levels and whatever their position in the company.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It even extends the scope to employees in Statutory Boards and prescribed public sector employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In short, almost all workers, including all PMEs who are in a contract of service, will now benefit and have access to the ECT.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, the ECT consolidates the Labour Court, which henceforth will not exist and fills the current lacuna in that the Small Claims Tribunal does not hear employment-related claims and disputes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Parties are encouraged to resolve employment disputes amicably by requiring parties to go through mediation before their cases are heard by the ECT.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, the ECT will go beyond the existing coverage to what I call the 18/43 rule.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The positive impact would be that the many, who used to have to file a civil suit, can now save the costs of engaging counsel to pursue their contractual claims.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, it preserves the sanctity of tripartism and the unique tripartite framework via the setting up of TADM to advise and assist aggrieved employees in the entire claims journey.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fifth, I am glad Minister Lim shared that the ECT does not dilute the role of unions but complements and supports unionism.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Union membership is encouraged as unions can and should assist and represent union members through the ECT process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I initially wanted to request the Minister to confirm for the purposes of Hansard recording that union officials, staff and representatives can represent union members throughout the ECT process from mediation to ECT hearing as union representation is not specifically stated in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I wanted to confirm if it will be done via regulations, and am glad the Minister earlier shared that it is allowed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Having highlighted the five positive aspects of ECT, I submit five suggestions to further augment and do even better.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I call them the "5Es" and what do these "5Es" stand for?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Encompassing, Economical, Enforceable, Ease of Access and Effective.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On the whole, the coverage of ECT is now much wider than was previously the case under the Labour Court system which only applied to employees covered by the EA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As of now, there are 18 contractual and 43 statutory claims.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Or is it time to also review our EA again to relook at some of these dichotomies and whether they are still relevant, specifically, for the $4,500 limit which appears in the EA, to be removed, as even unions, too, face challenges from employers who often use this $4,500 as a proxy for scope of representation?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In a similar vein, I submit we should also review the EA and that the ECT be further stretched to cover possibly new categories of workers, such as professional freelancers who are workers themselves whether in temporary, full-time, part-time or other arrangements especially when these freelancers are more vulnerable than employees themselves who are currently protected by the EA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In addition, a point of clarification which I have is whether those under apprenticeship agreements, including interns will have recourse to the ECT.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I say this because we have many youths and even now new hires who are on such informal arrangements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are two steps when one takes on an ECT action.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The first would be the filing of claim and mediation and the second would be the actual ECT hearing after mediation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Though the actual costs and prescribed fees of both steps have not been articulated, I suggest that the fees and charges should be made affordable and not exorbitant so that all collars 	Page: 82 of workers can gain access.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For the second step of convening a hearing, the costs and fees should be reasonable and not deter workers who need to proceed for a hearing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the same time, all the charges must reflect and correspond to the claim amount, and sufficient safeguards must be in place to prevent the floodgates of frivolous, vexatious or unsupported claims.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is good that the Bill states that if the dispute is settled at mediation or tripartite mediation, the parties must enter into a settlement agreement in the prescribed form.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is in section 7(1) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Of course, whichever way, there is still the hassle of enforcing it by a writ of seizure and sale.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I certainly hope that the enforcement process can be further streamlined, made hassle-free, easier and economical so that the claimant would not be subjected to further stresses when the other party is rogue.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In fact, during yesterday's debate on the Administration of Justice Bill, I similarly urged that a more rigorous and robust enforcement regime be imposed for non-compliance of ECT judgments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The ECT as well as the upcoming TADM should be easily accessible to all workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In fact, the entire claims process from filing should be made simple and convenient for the layman.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Proper communications and cascading should be done such as simple infographics, workflow charts or pocket guides with frequently asked questions to explain the workings of the ECT and TADM in an easy to read and digestible manner in a variety of languages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I, therefore, urge MOM to ensure that the ECT bear this in mind and expedite hearings which are provided for in this Bill so as not to be an encumbrance to clear, genuine, needy claimants and their claims.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To add, it is recommended that presiding judicial officers of the ECT should be well-acquainted with employment and industrial relations issues and, in particular, unions and tripartism, so that they can be even more effective in carrying out their role in dispute resolution and adjudication.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   I support MOM's new Employment Claims Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It should (a) enable workers to save on legal fees and not end up spending too much; (b) expedite the mediation process and shorten case processing time for workers; (c) also streamline the administration procedures; and (d) be able to solve the cases speedily.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In English): In conclusion, I applaud the setting up of the ECT.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This watershed milestone offers even greater protection for workers in Singapore especially the PMEs who are a growing yet increasingly vulnerable segment of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It provides an inclusive, affordable and accessible advisory, alternative dispute resolution mechanism and adjudication.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The implementation of the ECT will also improve efficiency, shortening the time required to resolve a salary-related claim.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I welcome this move in making our labour laws more inclusive and efficient.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, I would like to raise four suggestions to further enhance this Bill so that it can be more encompassing and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, it opens a possibility that domestic workers may be included and I quote, "at a later date when operations have stabilised." In the meantime, affected domestic workers will have to, I quote, "approach their employment agencies and/or MOM to resolve disputes" as they are not covered by the EA and thus do not have access to the Labour Court.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If they are not covered from the start, requiring them to approach MOM would perpetuate all the downsides of their current claims dispute settlement mechanism that the ECT is trying to resolve.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As such, I propose that the Ministry indicate the public timeline for domestic workers to be included in the overall operations of the ECT.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Thus, I would like to propose that the ECT should preferably deal with claims related to discrimination based on age, disability, race, gender and unfair dismissal.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This will bring it in line with other jurisdictions, such as the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Including claims related to other workplace grievances will make the ECT more comprehensive and useful for employees.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To be inclusive in this instance is to facilitate access to the ECT, in particular, for those are less fortunate in our midst.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Access to any legal recourse should be made accessible to all, regardless of their financial circumstances.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is the point that Members in this House will concur with.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such cost can be prohibitive, especially for low-wage 	Page: 84 workers, some of whom may not even have received their salaries for a period of time.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The ECT sets out to, I quote, "create a more accessible system" for potential employees who wish to seek redress, and higher costs may lower accessibility.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Hence, as my third proposal, I would like to propose that the grounds of decision by the ECT be made free to claimants so that they can better understand the factors considered by the ECT and thus be more aware of their rights.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This can also help them decide on further actions they may wish to undertake.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Notes of evidence should also be made more affordable, with charges waived for low-income claimants.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Madam, the move to replace the Labour Court with the ECT was based on two main considerations, that is, to have more inclusivity and, secondly, to enhance efficiency in reaching resolutions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I welcome the move to make labour laws more inclusive and efficient.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, I would like to make some suggestions to further enhance this Bill, so that it can be more inclusive.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The first thing that I would like to touch on is related to costs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am quite concerned that the cost incurred to use the ECT's services may become an obstacle that causes workers, especially low-wage workers, to become reluctant to step forward and make their claims.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The issue of cost should not become an impediment for anyone who wishes to obtain any legal service.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Hence, with the implementation of the ECT, I would like to request that the Ministry reduce the costs that will be incurred and provide waivers for low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In the Ministry's Consultation Paper, it was stated under paragraph 8 that the ECT was implemented only as an "expeditious mechanism to deal with salary-related claims".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, it does not include other aspects like job dismissals that were conducted unfairly or due to discrimination.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Here, Madam, I hope that the ECT can also include claims made by workers that are related to, firstly, issues of discrimination due to age, disability, religion, race, gender and, secondly, dismissals that were conducted unfairly.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It cannot be denied that issues of discrimination and unfair dismissals still occur in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in 2013, the then-Acting Minister for Manpower, Mr Tan Chuan-Jin, said that between 2007 and 2013, MOM received, on average, 70 cases from female workers every year, whereby 70% of them were expectant mothers who felt that they were dismissed unfairly.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, Madam, I believe that the ECT can become more encompassing and, therefore, bring about more benefits and become more meaningful to workers, if claims related to issues of discrimination and unfair dismissals can be included in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In English): Madam, in conclusion, on the basis of these four proposals I have shared earlier in enhancing the working of this Bill, I support the setting up of the ECT.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement welcomes the Ministry's effort in establishing the ECT to provide a more accessible system that can resolve salary-related claims more affordably and quickly for more employees compared to the current Labour Court.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That said, there are some clarifications and suggestions that I would like to make from the perspective of low-wage workers and vulnerable workers that the Ministry could look into.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Currently, separate claims have to be filed to CPF Board for their owed CPF payments.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is taxing on their time, resources and morale.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since most salary claims are very likely to include CPF payments, making it possible to file both these claims will provide them with better assurance and more efficient work processes.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, I would like the Ministry to clarify section 22 subsection 2(a) in the Employment Claims Bill.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More specifically, how do we define when claims are deemed frivolous and vexatious and what are the considerations involved?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In helping workers with salary grievances, U-Care Centre (UCC) has helped low-wage workers with claims as low as $50.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would these cases count as vexatious or frivolous?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In section 4 for Conduct of Mediation Sessions, the Bill currently does not stipulate a time frame as a guideline for mediation cases to be resolved, which I believe can open a loophole for exploitation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Fourth, I would like to seek clarification and confirmation that the Bill would allow for another person, such as next-of-kin, unionists, UCC consultants and others, to make the claim on behalf of the affected employee especially for workers who may not be intellectually sound but may still be able to stay gainfully employed.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: UCC had come across salary grievance cases involving workers with intellectual disability.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that having a provision to allow representation for workers with some disability can be beneficial to these groups of people who may otherwise not be able to capitalise on the ECT's role in resolving salary disputes.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Likewise, as an extension, I would like to confirm the provisions under sections 18 and 19 with regard to the representation of employees who are non-union members during the ECT.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There will be claimants who may not have the capacity and knowledge which may hinder their capabilities to fully represent themselves adequately during mediation or tribunals.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I would like to seek clarification whether the Bill will allow non-union members making the claim to have officers from the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) help centres, such as UCC, to follow through on such cases of salary dispute.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workers who earn $2,000 and below should be given a waiver so as not to create such a financial strain upon themselves as they are claiming what should have been rightfully theirs to begin with.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Page: 86 Lastly, I would like to make some operational suggestions that may ensure that the ECT can benefit as many Singaporeans as possible who need their services.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In UCC's experience in dealing with low-wage workers, there are three factors that have been extremely beneficial for these workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These three factors cover working hours, claim forms drafted in the various vernacular languages, and ramping up outreach and publicity efforts.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, claim forms should also be in vernacular languages and the claimant should be given an option to request for officers who can speak in their preferred language or dialect.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Third, I would like to urge the Ministry to ramp up outreach efforts to educate and inform workers on the ECT.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Ministry should look into embarking on strong publicity efforts on educating workers, especially the low-wage, vulnerable workers, on the newly-formed tribunal.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At this juncture, I also call for the Ministry to continue giving support to centres that assist employees with workplace advisory like NTUC's UCC, Centre for Domestic Employees (CDE) that could render assistance to our maids, UPME Centre and Migrant Workers' Centre (MWC).

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such help centres can play an instrumental role in creating greater awareness about the ECT.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, please allow me to conclude in English.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications and suggestions that I have made to improve the work processes and accessibility of the ECT to workers in seeking redress for salary disputes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The working people of Singapore regardless of nationality, type of job, union membership, age or gender, require a channel for fair and just hearing and judgment that calls for social justice.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is, indeed, timely that our workers be provided with an inclusive, accessible, expeditious and fair trial for employment claim matters for any specified employment dispute concerning the recovery of salary, re-employment or where an employment relationship has ceased.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, workers in non-unionised industry sectors will largely benefit from this tribunal.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, I have a few clarifications to raise and hope the Minister will provide further clarity.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In order to allow for a mediation process as the first line of amicable settlement, the mediation proceeding is seen to be set as a precursor before one proceeds to the ECT at the discretion of the Commissioner.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The mediation process must be encouraged and supported for a win-win outcome.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There are presently various different mediation routes to cater for various distinct classes of workers, as mentioned earlier by the Minister.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: MOM's mediation service for employees covered 	Page: 87 under the EA is one.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The second is TMF covered under the IRA for employees who are union members working in non-unionised companies.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: And the third is MOM's conciliation service for unions and unionised companies as per provision under the IRA.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, the Bill could have been made clearer as to how mediation through TMF should proceed in the ECT.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The question I would like to ask the Minister is: will all cases be referred to the ECT mediation process, regardless of whether the claimant is a union member or not?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If yes, will all unions then have to go through exemptions ordered by the Minister in order to represent our members at the mediation stage?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In terms of representation at the tribunal under section 18, section 34(1)(d) does not apply, that is, the Minister may not order for exemption to allow for union representation at the tribunal.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, earlier, the Minister did mention that unions can represent members at the tribunal.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, the Bill does not state this clearly, so I hope there is more clarity to this.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The question is: how was the limit set and why was there a limit in the first place?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If the limit is not specified in the Bill, does it mean that it can be varied?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can the claimant file for separate proceedings if he or she has multiple claims of different forms?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For example, if claimant has already filed for a case on his overtime pay for a few thousand dollars, will he be able to file for another hearing for his bonus payment?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What happens if there is a deadlock during the ECT proceedings or parties disagree with the decision of the tribunal?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Is appeal to High Court through section 23 the only available route?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can a union member, on the advice of the union, proceed further to IAC instead?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The tribunal magistrates, who are specialised in this process, do they have any experience on labour matters?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If not, will this be a concern and how will it be addressed?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In most cases of employees making claims, there is a time bar to the extent of their claims whereas, in the case of employers making recovery of overpayments, there is no similar time bar imposed.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Does this time bar apply to both employers and employees making similar claims, for example short payment or over payment of overtime pay?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What happens if the ECT orders a company to pay up to the three months' pay, but thereafter the company refuses, how should the claimant proceed?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will the company be liable and subject to penalty or will the tribunal demand for the payment to be made good by the employer, such as in the form of instalment payment or payment recovered by Writ of Seizure and 	Page: 88 Sale of Asset?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The other clarifications I would like to make is: will the ECT address claims under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Regulations in section 34 of the Bill leaves this question open.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As much of the evidence that employees need to prove their claim would often be in the hands of employers, can the tribunal draw an adverse inference where the employer is not forthcoming with that information so as to facilitate access to evidence?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Section 10 of the Bill seems to be silent on the contents of the record of the tribunal and whether parties are entitled to a copy of this record.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It seems a stark contrast to section 13(2) of the Small Claims Tribunals Act, where another Court under the same cluster which the ECT will be in, which expressly fleshes out the above.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Should the Bill go even further than section 13(2) of the Small Claims Tribunal Act and require written reasons for decisions?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill is a welcome relief for workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am sure there will be many refinements down the road to ensure that workers get paid their rightful salaries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For now, I have a few issues that I would like to put to the Minister to address.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The setting up of the tribunal finally recognises that compelling PMEs to file their claims with the civil Courts can be lengthy and costly, thus discouraging PMEs from pursuing their just compensation and creating the unintended consequences of protecting unscrupulous employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, what is the purpose of differentiating the claims limit between the two types of claimants, and why give a higher allowance to claimants going through the TMF or MOM conciliation when these claimants have more alternative avenues to resolve their salary-related issues?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 12, subsection 8, gives the Government the flexibility to prescribe different classes of employees and employers and different claim limits for different classes of claimants and different circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rather than prescribe different classes in terms of whether they go directly to the 	Page: 89 tribunal or through the TMF, I believe the logical thing to do, given the differentiated employment market, is to prescribe different classes of claimants according to their salary range and set the different claim limits accordingly to ensure inclusive coverage of PMEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Better still, to ensure fairness to all workers, would the Minister consider a more dynamic claims limit that is pegged to six months of the claimant's last drawn salary or $30,000, whichever is higher?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The claims limit should not be pegged to the claims limit of the Small Claims Tribunal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employment claims are by nature, complexion and quantum dissimilar to small commercial claims.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is very important that we send a signal to employers and employees alike that employment claims are not small claims.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second issue is the time limit to submit a mediation request.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 3, subsection 2, sets out two different timings for claimants: (a) six months after the last day of employment for disputes where an employment relationship has ended; or (b) one year after the occurrence of the dispute for other disputes, presumably where the employment relationship has not ended.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This seems anomalous, as I would expect the majority of cases to fall under the former category where the employment relationship has ended.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The six-month timing is, therefore, potentially disadvantageous to the majority of claimants and also adds an extra burden on workers who find themselves in the unfortunate situation of becoming unemployed and in an acrimonious salary dispute with their former employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe the Government can be more liberal and understanding of the situation faced by unemployed workers by extending the timing from six months to one year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will also equalise the timings among the different specified employment disputes under clause 3, subsection 2, making it fair to all workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third issue is the question of representation before the tribunal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 5 specifies that claimants must act in person and cannot be represented by an advocate and solicitor or by an agent, paid or otherwise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, an officer or full-time employee could represent employers for the dispute.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a potential imbalance here that would disadvantage claimants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Companies could send their in-house lawyers or professional HR professionals at no cost to them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In such a situation, PMEs would also be disadvantaged, not to mention rank-and-file workers and foreign workers hampered by language differences and lack of knowledge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Discretionary powers should be given to the tribunal to allow claimants representation by advocates or agents when it is apparent that the claimants are at a disadvantage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fourth issue is the question of enforcement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 22, subsection 11, states that a claims order made by the tribunal might be enforced in the same manner as that made by a District Court.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is apparent from this that enforcement of the claim orders could be a major problem going forward and active enforcement on the part of the Ministry is the only way to minimise the problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister said in his 2015 reply that the Ministry is looking into enhancing the protection for workers in this regard more holistically.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could we get an update on how the Ministry intends to do this to minimise non-compliance with claim orders?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, concerning the public consultation on the Bill that closed on 23 March this year, the summary of key comments received and the Ministry's responses were not published on the 	Page: 90 feedback unit's Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH) website or the Ministry's website as promised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Notwithstanding the above issues, this setting up of the ECT is a good beginning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is true in all three major sectors, even construction, which saw its PMET proportion just exceed 50% in 2015.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It comes as no surprise, therefore, that PMETs are also increasingly represented among the unemployed and those laid off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In 1990, the proportion of PMETs in the resident workforce was just half the 2015 figure; the proportion in manufacturing just a third of the 60% it has climbed to by 2015.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Through such rapid changes, the economy continued to maintain very low levels of unemployment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Policymakers have been alert to the challenges arising from the rapidly changing composition of the workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As the Minister for Manpower revealed at this year's Committee of Supply debate, his Ministry's approach in implementing these initiatives has become increasingly direct and oriented towards the individual jobseeker's needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But jobs do not appear out of thin air.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A labour market framework that facilitates job creation is needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The recognition of this overall framework for employment has to evolve to match the needs arising from these changes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And this is exactly what the Bill today signifies ‒ an advance in our labour market framework.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In January 2015, Parliament passed the Industrial Relations (Amendment) Bill to extend union representation to PMETs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In August 2015, Parliament voted overwhelmingly on an amendment to the EA, which obliged employers to ensure that each employee is provided with properly written or electronic records of individual employment terms and salary payments and deductions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The current Bill builds on that kind of momentum.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The ultimate aim of setting up the ECT should be to strengthen HR practices among employers, and further improve labour standards in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: When realised, such benefits will accrue broadly to all labour market participants, not just PMETs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The process for making employment claims should ultimately contribute to the strengths of Singapore's labour market, not weaken them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Complicated legislation raises the costs of adjudication and enforcement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If the employment claims process becomes difficult and costly for employers and employees, each and every dispute could potentially turn into a minefield and end 	Page: 91 up benefiting no one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: To prevent these kinds of issues, a robust framework for making employment claims should ensure that all parties in any dispute progress towards a resolution in as expeditious a manner as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What is undesirable is to have a process which is unable to convince all parties concerned that a clear resolution has been reached.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If any party to a dispute thinks matters are unresolved and continues to hold out for more, the delays will clog the claims system and the ensuing gridlock from delayed resolution will, ultimately, have negative consequences for the economy as a whole.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is also important to consider the lot of small businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A clear and straightforward framework will benefit them as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike larger enterprises, small businesses which do not have the benefit of dedicated HR and legal departments may see a rise in business costs if the risks of employment disputes increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The first point is on whether the role of unions can be expanded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Why does the role of unions appear limited?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I know the Minister has just clarified that tripartite mediation advisors can attend as observers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that this is a significant start and I am glad to see that it has been included.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What I am thinking of is a much more active role for unions mainly because, with union participation, you will get a balance between calls for inclusivity and the need to preserve efficiency in the tribunal's workings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The union movement has been at the forefront of the call for such a tribunal and is in the best position to actually help increase the efficiency of these processes while at the same time improving inclusivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The role of union representatives or resource persons should be formalised for cases which come before the tribunal after mediation has failed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: My second question is on the claims cap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The claims cap now clearly allows more workers, including PMETs, to avail themselves of the tribunal as an avenue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If we consider the usual notice periods set into contracts for termination, the current caps on claims appear to have been well thought out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But if contractual bonus payments are allowed, then the claims cap becomes limiting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: My last question is on guidelines for awards by the tribunal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What will guide the tribunal in its decisions and what should the tribunal not take into account in making awards?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What is the process by which award guidelines are formulated?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Would a body which has expertise in wage negotiations, such as the National Wages Council or SNEF, be permitted to comment about what the tribunal should take into account?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: After all, the tribunal's role is adjudication, not policy-making.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, allow me to highlight five areas of concern.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While most parties are expected to act in person before the tribunal, the new Bill allows for certain individuals to be exceptions to this rule.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify who these individuals will be?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: According to section 23 of the Small Claims Tribunal Act, certain parties need not act in person at Small Claims Tribunal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This includes low-wage elderly workers who have received little formal education and have a poor command of English.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This group of vulnerable individuals should also be protected at the ECT.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In such cases, there is usually a significant power differential between employees and employers, even if interpreters are provided.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Allowing them representation or assistance by solicitors, agents or McKenzie friends will ensure fair outcomes are achieved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act has not been included.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister explain the rationale for its exclusion?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Leaving out this Act would mean depriving migrant workers of protections offered to them for salary-related claims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, on the rules of evidence, under the EA, there have been reports of inconsistent practices at the Labour Court as to the types of evidence and witness testimonies accepted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was previously pointed out that Labour Court Commissioners have refused to accept material evidence, such as video recordings of employers confessing to non-payment of salary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under clause 33(2) of the new Bill, Rules of Court provide for the summoning of witnesses and provision of evidence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be helpful if formal and clear rules can be put in place and publicised as to what types of evidence and testimonies are admitted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would help claimants when preparing their cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fourthly, I would like to highlight the need for stronger enforcement of Court orders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: According to charity workers, low-wage employees currently face difficulties when trying to enforce Labour Court orders or settlements obtained at the mediation stage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Although legal mechanisms, such as a Writ of Seizure and Sale, are available, these involve high costs and are usually out of reach of low-wage employees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In order to avoid payment, charities have reported that it is common for employers to declare bankruptcy and wind up their companies, only to set up a new company under a new name.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One such model is Hong Kong's Protection of Wages on Insolvency Ordinance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On access to grounds of decision which a previous Member has mentioned, clause 10 of the Bill provides for a registry to keep all records of the tribunal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, unlike section 13 of the Small Claims Tribunal Act, it does not explicitly state that these records will be available to parties upon application.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if records will be made available?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Page: 93 Access to grounds of decision is important to allow employees to make informed decisions on further action to take.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if this sum will be made more affordable?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The proposed constitution on the ECT to decide on employment claims as proposed under this Employment Claims Bill is, indeed, a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have a few concerns which I hope the Minister can address.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, I note that the Bill will only deal with salary-related claims, not other types of claims or grievances related to work or workplace.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, there is no specific tribunal to address such issues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOM has, in previous years, acknowledged that there are such cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not overlook the issues of unfair dismissal or discrimination.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And discrimination can involve different kinds of discrimination.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should look to the examples of other first world countries, like the UK, which has an employment tribunal handling all types of claims for quite some time now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unfair dismissal or discrimination could well form part of the factual matrix in some of the cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How would the tribunal handle submissions or evidence on such issues?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may well be unfair to parties in such cases for the appointed tribunals to just ignore arguments relating, for example, to unfair dismissal or discrimination.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is naive to pretend that such scenarios will not happen and it may be an injustice to employees or employers if the tribunal were to disregard such issues or evidence completely.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This may take away some cases from the Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can have a tribunal that hears claims or employment claims, unfair dismissal and discrimination as well.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague, Mr Faisal Manap, as well as other speakers before me have proposed that domestic workers should also be considered to be entitled to the use of the ECT.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By way of example, the Employment Tribunal in the UK hears claims from employees arising from unlawful 	Page: 94 treatment by employers, potential employers or even trade unions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unlawful treatment includes unfair dismissal, discrimination and unfair deductions from one's pay.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill provides that claims must be filed for mediation within one year from the date on which the claim arises, or six months if the employment relationship has ended.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could the Minister explain the rationale for having such a short time limit under the Bill, especially that of half a year?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister consider raising the limits to at least one year after the employment relationship has ended?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have asked this because six months is really a short time and it could well be that the employee was busy looking for a new job, adjusting to a new job or his or her family may require urgent attention or, as we often see in employment disputes, the employee may be communicating with his or her employers and trying to come to an agreement regarding the dispute.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am of the view that, unlike the Small Claims Tribunal, we should set a higher minimum monetary limit for cases before the ECT.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A good indication of a minimum limit should be the median annual income so that employers are less likely to be able to delay a hearing before the tribunal on a calculation that the employee may not have sufficient resources to pursue the case in the civil Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, the claim limit should be raised beyond $20,000.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let it cover more claims involving more PMEs and PMEs with higher income rather than let it go to the State Courts or beyond, where legal costs would be considerably higher.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 21 of the Bill provides that a tribunal is not bound by the rules of evidence in the conduct of any proceeding and may inform itself on any matter in such a manner as the tribunal thinks fit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is something which I feel is not satisfactory.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If, as what I suggested earlier that the claims limit can be increased beyond $20,000, we should definitely enhance the current provision in clause 21 of letting the tribunal not be bound by the rules of evidence in proceedings under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am saying this because, under the proposed provisions, the tribunal has a wide discretion whether to admit or accept evidence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The risk of a tribunal failing to consider relevant evidence or making its decision based on arguably wrongful evidence cannot be discounted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I feel that this affects the quality of justice.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Naive or less educated workers who may not know how best to protect themselves with written evidence or any agreement with the employers may be disadvantaged by such a system.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This problem of the tribunal not bound by the rules of evidence is further compounded by other provisions in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, clause 23 provides that appeal against any decision of the tribunal is to the High Court but only on issue of law or a claim being outside the jurisdiction of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why do we not accept further evidence, especially if further evidence turns up after the proceedings?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, first I would like to declare that I am an employer.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, conflicts only need to be settled because there are conflicts.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We hope that employers and employees could find a way to smoothen their communication channels to avoid unnecessary conflict.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some SMEs have no HR departments, and the work of HR s is usually handled by the Administration Department, or personally taken charge of by the boss himself.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: PMETs will be implicated under the new legislation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Since most PMETs are well-educated, dealing with them is very different from that of blue-collar workers, in terms of concept and process.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I really hope that this Bill could form a standard reference for HR management and that employers and PMETs could fully understand the content to avoid getting into conflicts which are impossible to mediate.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, I also hope that the ECT could accurately assess which claims are reasonable and which are not reasonable at all.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Local enterprises are all facing severe manpower shortage and, due to economic restructuring, every trade and industry is trying to reshuffle its resources.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs also hope to take the opportunity to recruit more PMETs and fully utilise their potential.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, if PMETs and employers can work together cordially, enterprises do not need to waste time and energy to address these conflicts, which only ends up aggravating the situation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I also have some concerns regarding the salary-related claims to be handled by the ECT.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Within the company, any personnel changes, including promotions, demotions, organisational restructuring, performance appraisals, retrenchments, resignations, and other management issues, are all eventually salary-related.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Such cases should be carefully dealt with at the ECT, to avoid being abused by employees.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Page: 96 Therefore, the tribunal will provide such employees with quicker and relatively cheaper options of dispute mechanisms than having to commence a suit in the civil Courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I take the opportunity to highlight and seek clarification on the following four areas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, section 19 of the Bill requires that parties to proceedings before the tribunal must act in person.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A similar provision exists for mediation under section 5 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A body corporate may be represented by its officer or full-time employee, but parties cannot be represented by an advocate and solicitor.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is understandable given that the objective of the tribunal is to provide a cost-effective mechanism to resolve the specified employment disputes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While I acknowledge that the tribunal is likely to play a more inquisitorial role than the civil Courts in adjudicating the specified employment disputes, I am concerned that in certain situations, there may be an "inequality of arms" between an employer and employee before the tribunal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would arise if an employer should be represented before the tribunal by a legally-trained employee.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I gather from the Minister today that he intends to allow union members to be represented by union representatives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The quantum of a claim per se is not indicative of the complexity of the claim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While the majority of cases before the tribunal are contemplated to be straightforward claims, there could be cases involving legal and factual complexity, for example, where a dispute requires an interpretation of terms or where an employment contract with a Singaporean is governed by a law other than Singapore law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In such cases, the tribunal would benefit from proper representation of parties' respective cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A possible way to address such cases is to allow the tribunal to appoint an assessor on an ad hoc basis, somewhat analogous to section 33 of the State Courts Act which allows a District Judge to, if he thinks fit, on the application of any party, or his own Motion, summon to his assistance a person of skill and experience in the matter to act as an assessor.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is also similar to the approach adopted in section 60 of the South Australian Employment Tribunal Act 2014 which allows the tribunal to refer any question arising in any proceedings to a special referee for the purpose of procuring a decision or opinion which the tribunal may or may not adopt.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This suggestion may, in part, at least, address an issue raised by the hon Member Mr Zainal Sapari when he highlighted the plight of employees suffering from certain disabilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, I support the objectives of requiring parties to mediate their employment disputes first before their cases may be heard by the tribunal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In most cases, this would be the most efficient dispute resolution mechanism as highlighted by the Minister just now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The UK also has a similar procedure, under section 18A of the Employment Tribunals Act 1996 Notwithstanding the benefits of mediation, I highlight that in one specific situation, the requirement of compulsory mediation imposed by the Bill may pose a disadvantage to the employee, by way of an example, where an employee has unsuccessfully mediated a specified employment dispute, such as leave entitlement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He has lodged the claim with the tribunal for that dispute, but before that claim is heard by the tribunal, the employer acts in a manner that gives rise 	Page: 97 to a second specified employment dispute, such as withholding salary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the Bill, the occurrence of the second specified employment dispute is one that the employee would have to submit a fresh mediation request.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In such a situation, it appears that the compulsory mediation of the second dispute would lead to duplication of resources and be less cost-effective, contrary to the objectives of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It would be more cost- and resource-efficient for the tribunal to be able to deal with both disputes at the same time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, while the tribunal is empowered under section 18(5) of the Bill to hear the two claims together, this would result in a delay to the employee having to obtain redress for both claims as he would have to wait until the second dispute has been mediated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A way to deal with such a situation is to empower the tribunal, upon the application of a party, to order the second dispute to be heard without a claim referral certificate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is what the UK has done by way of its Employment Tribunals (Early Conciliation: Exemptions and Rules of Procedure) Regulations 2014.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Thirdly, whilst the creation of the tribunal to hear salary-related monetary claims would allow employees to resolve employment disputes more quickly, an unintended effect may be the added complexity because of the potential overlaps in the roles of the tribunal, Commissioner for Labour and the Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Section 16 of the Bill thus seeks to minimise such multiplicity of proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Could the Minister please clarify what is the rationale of this subsection?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This provision, on surface, seems odd for a few reasons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mediations encourage amicable settlement of disputes by encouraging parties to speak freely about their issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And it has been very successful, as the Minister observed earlier.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Parties are usually assured that what is discussed during mediation will not be used against them in a subsequent claim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Further, parties are generally discouraged from relying on or referring to their strict legal positions at mediation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, Part II of the Bill which deals with mediation of employment disputes, does not require an employer to raise the defences he wishes to rely on at the mediation stage.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If no such requirement is imposed, would it not be inconsistent for section 16(7) of the Bill to preclude an employer from relying on a defence that it is not required to raise the same during mediation?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third, given that mediation under the Bill is to be conducted in private and, in general, discussions between the parties during mediation are private and confidential, how would the 	Page: 98 tribunal be apprised of what was discussed during the mediation, given that it was not present at the mediation?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In April this year, the EA was enhanced to facilitate better administrative records and for employees to better understand employment terms and benefits.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Though I agree that not all complaints and claims should be viewed with a negative light, lest we think the current job market is skewed with unbridled bad practices, the need to continue pushing for a fair and inclusive workplace behooves us to look at these areas where current coverage is lacking and has to be enhanced.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And since the primary purpose of the proposed Employment Claims Bill is to facilitate the expeditious resolution of employment disputes by providing mediation for such disputes, there should be prior steps made available that assist employees to make informed decisions or assessments of whether they should raise their cases and how best for those, as covered under the Act, not to overburden our mediation system.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: So, here, I would like to highlight three areas that I urge MOM to review and consider.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The first area, increasing employees' awareness of employment terms and basic legal structure of contracts and service agreements.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Annually, we have fresh cohorts of graduates who are looking to join the workforce at around this time of the year.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many of them would be delighted to have been gainfully employed and offered an employment even before they graduate.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But how many of us would recall our first ever employment contract and what it really contains?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To most who are hired as permanent employees, they may remember having signed a contract that contains pages of information and, at best, they would likely take interest in remembering a 	Page: 99 few things, such as their monthly salary, bonus scheme, annual leave and maybe termination notice period.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On one hand, we can say this is a blessing as one should really not have to focus on the contract details regularly when they are contentedly engaged in their day jobs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But on the contrary, when an unfortunate situation does arise, it may be a difficult and costly affair for some of them who did not fully understand what they had been contractually bound from the start.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While it is useful that the enhanced EA mandates stipulating these key employment terms (KET) in writing, but the administration of KET does not necessarily reduce the misunderstandings or even minimise disputes that arise.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I suggest that MOM consider with the Workforce Development Agency or now Workforce Singapore and SkillsFuture agencies, to providing access on basic knowledge related to contracts, service agreements, common HR practices to all working age adults so that they are better equipped with understanding the latest industry practices and mentally prepared to handle these situations when they arise.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will also be useful for those undertaking part-time work, mature workers or workers who are transiting back to the workforce, fresh graduates and those workmen who are not covered under any industries specified under the WorkRight initiative.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This way, for those who are not covered under the EA or will not benefit from the Employment Claims Bill currently, they will be more aware and better informed to ask the right questions during contract negotiation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is the first step in preventing them from getting into the unknowns.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The second area, provision of support during and after the claim mediation period.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Often, we assume that all these workers who have been unfairly dismissed or treated at work will eventually be duly compensated when their cases are proven and supported.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, many do not know that the consequences of a worker being unfairly dismissed, mistreated or suddenly dismissed goes way beyond the monetary compensations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some of the downsides include the difficulty of being re-hired due to uncertainty by their prospective hiring companies as to why they have been dismissed in the first place, long waiting periods for professionals to search for equivalent matching jobs, diminishing self-confidence of those who are financially strapped during this claim period and an inability to cope after they have been reinstated post the findings and so on.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Personally, I have some residents who brought up cases of this nature at my Meet-the-People sessions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The first case is that of a resident in her early 40s.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Before she was laid off, she held the position of HR Director in a multinational corporation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Her dismissal was not due to misconduct or even restructuring, but she was at the end of the fifth month into her first pregnancy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One would imagine that she would know how to handle the situation because of her background in HR and the fact that she is a senior manager.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On the contrary, she was devastated and tried to seek help.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But she had no avenues to turn to, and the EA excludes her from any coverage for the mere fact of her salary range.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: So, though the company did compensate her financially in the end, she was physically not prepared to fight for her rights, which she believed she was justified to have even more of.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And the costly process gave her second thoughts because the child was going to be due soon.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Searching for a job after her maternity leave would be a second challenge for her as she juggles between her new-born baby and seeking a job of a similar scope and seniority.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: He is aware that he has not been appropriately paid for some of the components in his work package and the matter has come to the attention of the company because there is a group of similar workers just like him a few years ago.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While some of his colleagues have had their packages duly adjusted and they have been paid for the missing monies, it was not so for him.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But because he is the sole breadwinner in his family and he has minimal paper qualifications, 	Page: 100 he is afraid of losing his job if he stresses upon this any further with his HR.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: So, how can MOM assist this group of individuals?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The last area, the path of pursuit in terms of the promotion of all these concepts, implementation and enforcement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: TAFEP, I recognise, is putting in efforts to expand and play a very key role in changing the mindsets of employers and HR practitioners, so that you build a good workplace architecture in order to get a fair and progressive workplace.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
